title: Sirhind victory day
hookLine: in May, Sikhs mark Banda Singh Bahadur's victory at Chappar Chiri
tomorrow: The ninth Guru and his three companions

lines: A FIELD ON THE ROAD TO SIRHIND.
cards: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh: the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory. On one early-summer day, that greeting carries extra weight on a field on the road to Sirhind.
Kirtan rises, steam lifts from the langar pots, and the sangat sits down together.

This is Chappar Chiri, where Banda Singh Bahadur's army met the forces of Wazir Khan, the governor whose order had ended the lives of Guru Gobind Singh's youngest sons. Sikh memory waited a long time for that day.
Now the field holds a fair.

teach.b: This path has already stood on this field and walked into Sirhind with Banda Singh. Today's question is how the day is kept. In Sikh memory, the winter order at Sirhind was a wound that stayed open.
When Wazir Khan fell at Chappar Chiri and the city was taken, that long wait ended. So the day is marked with joy, with kirtan and langar.
But justice and revenge are not the same word. Revenge is about what I want back. Justice, in the Sikh telling, is about wrong being answered.
The line is not we got even. It's justice came, and the victory, as the greeting says, belongs to Waheguru, not to any commander. There's a deeper court, too.

In the Japji, Guru Nanak's morning prayer, the thirty-fourth stanza describes the realm of dharam, where, in paraphrase, each person is judged by their own deeds, and true is the One, and true is the court.
On that view, no human victory is the last word.

And the honest telling: historians record that the city's people suffered when Sirhind was taken. A fair account keeps that too. So the day is kept with joy, but it doesn't become a day to hate anyone living now.
The boys in the tower aren't brought back by any battle.
What came was justice, not repair.

how: Sikhs mark the victory at Chappar Chiri with kirtan, Ardas and langar, and some gather at Chappar Chiri, where the battle was fought.

games.q: it's the day of the victory, and the sangat gathers at Chappar Chiri. how does today's telling hold the victory?
o: as justice that came, with the city's suffering kept honestly beside it.
games.why: justice came, and a fair telling doesn't hide that the city's people suffered. the true court, the Japji says, is still the One's.

practice: Bring to mind one wrong you've seen, near or far, that hasn't been answered; it might be small, someone blamed for what they didn't do, or it might be large.
Hold it without anger and ask what justice would look like here, not revenge, not getting even, just the wrong put right, and let the question sit without needing an answer.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and leave the rest to the true court.

wordCard.voice: Chappar Chiri. The field where Banda Singh Bahadur's army won the victory marked each year as Sirhind victory day, when a long wait for justice ended. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: fateh, victory, the word in the Sikh greeting that gives the victory to Waheguru.

carryVoice: Your line: justice came. The victory, as the greeting says, belongs to Waheguru. Until tomorrow.
